Nathanaël Berestycki Artificial intelligence (AI) is solving increasingly complex open mathematical problems at a faster pace than ever before. On 8 September 2026, OpenAI announced that their AI agents have made progress on parts of the Navier-Stokes equations. These are a set of maths problems formulated roughly 200 years ago that describe the movement of fluids. They are also one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems , seven highly complex unsolved mathematical problems carrying a prize of USD 1 million. This is the most noteworthy mathematical result produced by an AI so far , but it is not the only one. Since May 2026, when an OpenAI representative said its AI had disproved an 80-year-old conjecture by prolific mathematician Paul Erdős, news of long-standing open mathematical problems being solved with AI has been coming in thick and fast. Nathanaël Berestycki , professor of stochastics at the University of Vienna, compares the current moment to a tipping point in the field of mathematics, a phase transition where previously slow growth suddenly becomes explosive and unstoppable, much like the spreading of a rumour or viral content in social networks. "It’s a major revolution in the way we are going to do maths," he says. On 7 October 2026, news of the release of over 700 mathematical manuscripts and over 370 related result families by OpenAI broke , just as we were in the last stages of editing this article. This illustrates the unimaginable speed at which things are changing in mathematics right now, as major outstanding problems are being solved in batches. "Many of our most beloved problems were just solved, so it’s a bit gut wrenching," commented Berestycki. OpenAI's Navier-Stokes announcement has prompted intense discussion within the mathematical community, including concerns about academic competition and the role of AI companies in mathematical research. This includes allegations, which OpenAI denies , that the company focused their resources on solving Navier-Stokes ( reportedly spending the equivalent of over USD 22 million in tokens) after learning two other researchers, Tristan Buckmaster (NYU) and Levent Alpöge (Anthropic), were close to a breakthrough . The controversy has prompted an unusually public response from the mathematical community. Three days after OpenAI announced its Navier-Stokes news, 25 Fields Medallists, recipients of one of mathematics' highest honours, published an open letter titled A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics . In it they argued that using maths to test AI systems was "detrimental to the science of mathematics", speaking of a fundamental mismatch between commercial AI goals and scientific research and the broader negative impact on society. The next day, the Association for Human Mathematics was launched, which aims to "protect mathematics as a human endeavour against the threat of artificial intelligence". Over 700 members signed up in less than three weeks. Aside from the outcry, a larger impact of Navier-Stokes on the collaborative nature of maths is already being felt. "People are worried to discuss partial results publicly now because anyone in the audience can input them into an AI and if the problem is solved this way, years of a mathematician's work can just disappear in an instant," says Vera Fischer, associate professor in mathematics. Her newly formed research group Uncovering the Axioms of Mathematics (UnAxiMa) will be looking at the trustworthiness of AI-generated outcomes. This development is problematic because, contrary to the popular image of maths geniuses working in isolation, mathematical progress depends on researchers sharing partial results and discussing ideas. Berestycki's work illustrates the importance of such exchange. He heads up the research group Discrete Random Structures at the University of Vienna, which brings together researchers from combinatorics, probability and statistical mechanics, applying methods and concepts developed for one field to another to gain new insights. His work depends heavily on open communication. If mathematicians hold back from sharing their insights for fear their work will be fed into AI systems, the two mathematicians worry that ultimately mathematical progress will be hampered. This is not the first time mathematics is faced with a period of profound change. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, paradoxes in set theory and debates about the foundations of mathematics caused mathematicians to question exactly how mathematical objects and proofs should be defined and justified. The resulting upheaval of the field led to developments in logic and formalisation, which completely reshaped mathematics and led to new ways of thinking about certainty, proof and abstraction. The rise of AI raises a different but related question: what is the importance of human understanding when machines can generate increasingly sophisticated results at the press of a button? In a world increasingly focused on short-term wins and efficiency, another big question is whether AI could eventually automate humans out of the mathematical equation entirely. Where before it could take years, sometimes decades, to solve a single problem, AI is expected to soon be able to generate mathematical proofs at a faster pace than mathematicians can assess, understand or apply them, a phenomenon known as proof abundance . Yet, mathematics is more than the sum of its proofs. "There is a huge misunderstanding that mathematics is just about solving problems," says Fischer. "Maths goes far beyond this." According to Fischer, a new proof requires deep understanding of how things are related to each other. It is this deep understanding that has an impact on the overall development of mathematics, rather than just the final proof. Finding a new result simultaneously means discovering new techniques and methods. Eventually, often decades later, these new methods might find unexpected applications in other areas, such as physics, chemistry, biology or even medicine, explains Fischer. Berestycki agrees: "The point of maths was never just to produce proofs, it was to produce an understanding, structures and frameworks that other sciences can draw from." Even if AI proves countless great results on its own, he argues, you simply cannot subtract the human from the process of understanding new structures and what they are helpful for. One of Berestycki's early works has made its way into biology. He was trying to find the answer to a purely theoretical question called the speed of 'coming down from infinity'. It describes how quickly particles aggregate in a big bang-like event. Berestycki recalls: "It eventually yielded concrete formulae, called sampling formulae, for the genetic diversity in a species sample." As it turns out, Berestycki's work was particularly useful for species with high fecundity, that is with a very high number of offspring, such as mussels, Pacific oysters and certain types of shrimp. Such unexpected discoveries could disappear in an age of proof abundance, argues Fischer. "When confronted with many different proofs that we as mathematicians have not worked through, how do we recognise what matters? How do we develop the understanding necessary to apply the gained knowledge in a different context?" Fischer's work offers an example of unexpected discovery: part of her work involved studying the structure of the 'real line', a mathematical concept that describes the set of all real numbers pictured as an infinite straight line, and identifying different ways to measure the complexity of its infinite structures. Fischer and her collaborators discovered a completely new relationship between two of these measurements: one can never be larger than the other. This dependence was a highly surprising result, as the prevailing expectation in the mathematical community had been that the two quantities were entirely independent. Even more remarkably, the discovery had an effect for a third measurement. Combined with earlier work, it showed that the standard axioms of mathematics are silent on how two of those quantities compare: either one can be larger than the other. What is more, for Fischer focusing on a single theorem means missing the bigger picture. To her, maths is much more than any one specific result. "We talk a lot about our recent results, but it takes around 100 years of hindsight in order to see larger developments, such as the formalisation of mathematics in the early 20th century, where entirely new notions appeared over generations." Aside from that, Fischer explains that mathematics is open-ended. Rather than being a set of fixed problems, it develops continuously with new proofs unearthing yet more unanswered questions and mathematical problems. "Speaking of the end of mathematics is like saying all science is done. Yet, no one is claiming that," she says. Berestycki agrees: "I don't think this means the end of maths." This is due to a feedback loop in maths, where new knowledge is generated through constant re-examining and distilling existing knowledge to further develop it. "Reducing complex mathematical concepts to their core is where AI currently still falls short," Berestycki says. "Proofs are not enough to keep the loop going productively." One of his most cited papers and what he calls "probably one of the most important things I've done in maths" is an example of this process of distillation. He took a notoriously complicated theory, the Gaussian multiplicative chaos (GMC), and uncovered its underlying mechanism by borrowing a surprisingly simple approach from an entirely different area. To borrow an analogy from the world of art, Berestycki's work was akin to discovering the perspective grid behind a painting. It reveals how the picture is organised and gives other artists a practical structure that they can use when constructing entirely different paintings. Berestycki explains that "mathematical truths can be obscured by complicated proofs, which only experts can understand". Instead, a simple proof can be understood and used by other mathematicians outside of that speciality to work on their own problems. His work on this particular theory has been useful for a large number of people working in very different areas of maths: from Liouville Quantum Gravity in theoretical physics to number theory and random matrices (which describe spectra of heavy nuclei in physics) and even financial mathematics. When asked for her most pessimistic prognosis, Vera Fischer replied: "I worry that people will lose interest in maths because they misunderstand it to be a competition of increasingly powerful analytical thinking, as being about who can compute faster and who can get there first." Yet, as a self-described optimist, Fischer has hope that people can use AI tools in a positive way. "AI does have the potential of speeding up the process of mathematical discovery, but it really requires a lot of joint work between mathematicians and figuring out how we properly use these tools. This takes time." Nathanaël Berestycki also remains convinced that not all is bad news. "We will face a few turbulent years for sure. Many aspects of the job will have to be reinvented." However, he too is optimistic that AI can be used as a tool to enhance knowledge and understanding "if used appropriately and not as a way to generate publicity for a company or self-promotion for an individual." The debate reaches beyond mathematics. At its heart is a question about whether, as a society, we value only results and the bottom line or whether we want to create space for curiosity and discovery. It concerns how we balance efficiency with the slower processes of deep understanding and slow-moving collaboration. Fischer concludes: "This moment in time is indeed a reckoning with our values. Maths is a living subject and proofs are a stepping stone towards a much bigger end result, towards true progress and (as it is written on the Fields Medal) 'mastering the universe'. It is about the progress of humanity as a whole." He is speaker and PI at the special Research Network Discrete Random Structures. She is part of the new Emerging Fields programme Uncovering the Axioms of Mathematics (UnAxiMa), where she will be revisiting the very foundations of mathematics and investigating the reliability and trustworthiness of AI-generated outcomes.
